title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Concurrency Control
lesson:
When two clients try to modify the same record at once, the system needs a rule for who wins. Pessimistic concurrency control assumes conflicts are likely and prevents them up front: a transaction takes a lock on the row (for example SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) before reading it, holds the lock until commit, and any competing writer waits or fails. Conflicts can never produce a lost update, but locks cost throughput, hold resources while a client may be slow, and introduce the risk of deadlocks when transactions acquire locks in different orders.

Optimistic concurrency control assumes conflicts are rare and takes no lock while working. Each record carries a version number (or timestamp, or ETag). A client reads the record along with its version, does its work, then writes back with a condition such as UPDATE ... SET balance = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If another writer got in first, the version no longer matches, zero rows are updated, and the client detects the conflict and retries from a fresh read (or surfaces an error to the user). This is a compare-and-swap at the application level, and it is the same idea behind HTTP If-Match headers and conditional writes in many key-value stores.

The choice depends on contention. With low contention, optimistic control wins: no lock waits, no held resources across user think-time, and it works naturally across stateless services and long-lived edit sessions. Under high contention on a few hot rows, optimistic control degrades badly, because many transactions do work only to fail validation and retry, wasting effort; there pessimistic locking, or restructuring the data to reduce contention, is usually better.

Whichever you choose, the failure it guards against is the lost update: two transactions read the same value, both compute a new value, and the second write silently overwrites the first. Optimistic retries should be bounded and should re-read state rather than blindly re-apply a stale computation, and retried operations should be safe to repeat.

questions.prompt: How does optimistic concurrency control detect that another writer modified a record in the meantime?
options: It holds a row lock from the read until the write
It checks at write time that the record's version still matches the one that was read
It serializes all writes through a single leader thread
It compares the client's wall-clock time to the server's
questions.explanation: The conditional write (WHERE version = ?) only succeeds if nobody else has bumped the version since the read, so conflicts are detected at commit time rather than prevented by locks.

questions.prompt: Optimistic concurrency control works best when conflicts on the same record are frequent.
questions.explanation: Frequent conflicts mean many transactions fail validation and redo their work, which is why optimistic control suits low-contention workloads.

questions.prompt: The anomaly where two transactions read the same value and the second write silently overwrites the first is called a ____ update.
questions.explanation: A lost update occurs when a later write overwrites an earlier one that it never saw; both locks and version checks exist to prevent it.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an optimistic update that hits a conflict and recovers.
items: Retry the whole operation using the fresh data
Write back conditioned on the original version
Read the record and its version
Detect that zero rows were updated
questions.explanation: The client reads with a version, attempts a conditional write, notices the version check failed, and then retries from a fresh read.

questions.prompt: Which risk is specific to pessimistic locking and not to optimistic version checks?
options: Deadlocks between transactions acquiring locks in different orders
Retries after a failed conditional write
questions.explanation: Optimistic control holds no locks while working, so it cannot deadlock, whereas lock-holding transactions can wait on each other in a cycle.
